questions.stem: Children with severe celiac disease who remain untreated are at risk for which of the following?

evidence.quote: Short stature, shout it out, yes or no. Yes, folate deficiency. Ricketts. Everybody agrees? So it is all of the above.
Older children and adolescents often present with extraintestinal manifestations, such as short stature, neurologic symptoms, or anemia.

questions.note:
All of the above. Untreated celiac disease flattens the villi of the proximal small bowel, so nutrients aren't absorbed and a growing child pays for it in several ways. The professor went through each option in lecture (yes, yes, yes) and confirmed "all of the above."
Short stature is correct on its own: chronic malabsorption and failure to thrive stunt growth, and the lecture lists short stature as an extraintestinal sign in older children.
Folate deficiency is correct on its own: folate is absorbed in the proximal small bowel, the area celiac disease hits hardest, so folate and iron deficiency are common.
Rickets is correct on its own: fat malabsorption cuts vitamin D and calcium uptake, which leaves soft, poorly mineralized bone in children.

questions.stem: You suspect a patient has celiac sprue and perform a biopsy of the distal duodenum. Which of the following would you expect to see in the biopsy of a patient who indeed has celiac disease?
choices: Increased plasma cells in the lamina propria
Increased number of red blood cells in the lamina propria

evidence.quote: Decrease in trapithelial lymphocytes, increased plasma cells in the lamina propria, increased number of absorptive villi, increased number of RBCs in laminna propria. What do you think? B. Very good.

questions.note:
Increased plasma cells in the lamina propria. Gliadin drives a T-cell and B-cell immune response in the mucosa, so the lamina propria fills with chronic inflammatory cells, including plasma cells that make the anti-tTG and antiendomysial antibodies. The classic biopsy shows intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia and villous atrophy.
Decreased intraepithelial lymphocytes is backwards: celiac disease increases them.
Increased absorptive villi is also backwards: the villi are blunted and flattened, which is why absorption fails.
Extra red blood cells in the lamina propria would mean hemorrhage, which is not part of the celiac picture.

questions.stem: Which of the following symptoms is consistent with the classic presentation of a patient with celiac disease?

evidence.quote: So, infertility hepatitis is not common, so it could be between C and D. So I can tell you diarrhea is more common. That's a classic presentation.
The classic presentation in adults is diarrhea, which may be accompanied by abdominal pain or discomfort.

questions.note:
Chronic diarrhea. Flattened villi mean less surface for absorption, so the classic presentation is diarrhea or steatorrhea with weight loss, and failure to thrive in children. The professor narrowed it to osteoporosis versus diarrhea and picked diarrhea as the classic one.
Infertility is not a common celiac presentation.
Hepatitis is not typical. Mildly raised liver enzymes are listed only as a less common finding.
Osteoporosis does happen, from poor absorption of calcium and vitamin D, but it is a secondary presentation in adults, not the classic one.

questions.stem: Which best describes the direct role of HLA-DQ8 in celiac disease?
choices: It is a signal molecule for pain in the spinothalamic tract.
It increases GI motility, leading to diarrhea.
It decreases GI motility, leading to constipation.

evidence.quote: It facilitates immune response, do we agree? Right? And it has nothing to do with GI motility, neither increases nor decreases, so we can get rid of those.
So it is deaminated by this, and that allows interaction with HLADQ2 and DQ8. Again, do make a note of that. These are present on surface of antigen presenting cells.

questions.note:
It facilitates an immune response. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 are MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells that present deamidated gliadin peptides to gliadin-reactive CD4+ T cells, which sets off the mucosal inflammation. Carrying one of them is needed for celiac disease, but most carriers never develop it.
HLA molecules have nothing to do with pain signaling in the spinothalamic tract.
HLA-DQ8 does not act on GI motility in either direction. The diarrhea comes from villous damage and malabsorption.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease?

evidence.quote: So this is often on your elbows and knees and buttocks, and this actually has 100% association with celiac disease.

questions.note:
Dermatitis herpetiformis. It is an immune-mediated, itchy papulovesicular rash on the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees and on the buttocks, and it has a 100% association with celiac disease, even when there are no GI symptoms.
Dyshidrotic eczema causes itchy blisters on the palms and soles and is not linked to celiac disease.
Hives are a general allergic or urticarial reaction, not a celiac sign.
Erythema nodosum is the skin lesion of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease and UC), not celiac disease.

questions.stem: The primary management for patients with celiac disease is removal of gluten from the diet. A small percentage of patients may need which of the following pharmacological interventions to combat their autoimmune state?

evidence.quote: So, what do you think it is? B, right? Corticosteroid agents. So, usually, the diet should help them, but sometimes this is needed.

questions.note:
Corticosteroid agents. Celiac disease is autoimmune, so when a gluten-free diet alone doesn't control the inflammation, an immunosuppressant such as a corticosteroid is used. The professor noted the diet usually works but steroids are sometimes needed.
Chemotherapy is for cancer. Long-standing celiac disease does raise the risk of lymphoma and adenocarcinoma, but chemotherapy is not used to treat the autoimmune disease itself.
Antiviral therapy and antibiotics can be ruled out right away because celiac disease is not an infection. Antibiotics are the treatment for Whipple disease, which is.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?
choices: In Whipple disease, macrophage formation causes obstruction of the lymphatic system, leading to decreased reabsorption of chylomicrons and maldigestion of fats.
In SIBO, vitamin B12, thiamine, nicotinamide and folate deficiencies are common.
In dumping syndrome, accelerated movement of chyme into the duodenum leads to a hyperosmolar state of the partially undigested contents, causing osmotic diarrhea.
Removal of a large portion of the small bowel leads to a malabsorptive state called short bowel syndrome.

evidence.quote: In cyber, B12, thymine, nicotinamide, folate deficiencies are common. Do we agree? No, what is wrong with that? Folate, because bacteria can make folate. We don't really see that deficiency, and the remaining two are correct.

questions.note:
B is the incorrect statement, because of folate. In SIBO the overgrowing bacteria make folate, which then gets absorbed, so folate levels are normal or even high. The rest of B is right: bacteria eat B12 before it can be absorbed, and thiamine and nicotinamide deficiencies are common. The professor pointed to folate as the error.
A is true: Tropheryma whipplei fills the mucosa with foamy macrophages that block lymphatics, so chylomicrons can't leave the gut and fat is malabsorbed.
C is true: after gastrectomy, hypertonic chyme rushes into the duodenum and pulls water into the lumen, giving early cramping and osmotic diarrhea.
D is true: short bowel syndrome is malabsorption after resection of a large part of the small intestine, from Crohn disease, injury, cancer, or necrotizing enterocolitis in infants.

questions.stem: From the lecture's matching exercise: which condition is characterized by flattening/atrophy of villi, diarrhea and dermatitis herpetiformis?

evidence.quote: flattening atrophy of villi, diarrhea, dermatitis, herpetiformis, which one is that? Celiac

questions.note:
Celiac disease. Gluten triggers mucosal inflammation that flattens the villi, which causes malabsorption and diarrhea, and dermatitis herpetiformis is its skin sign.
Cystic fibrosis causes malabsorption through pancreatic insufficiency, not villous atrophy, and it does not cause dermatitis herpetiformis.
Whipple disease can blunt villi, but its hallmark is foamy macrophages blocking the lymphatics, and it has no skin rash like this.
SIBO causes fat malabsorption and B12 deficiency from bacterial overgrowth, usually because of slowed motility.
Short bowel syndrome is malabsorption from losing intestinal length to surgery.

questions.stem: From the lecture's matching exercise: which condition results from massive resection of the small intestine?

evidence.quote: Celiac, massive resection of small intestine. Short bowel syndrome
Removal of such large portion of the small bowel leads to a malabsorptive state called as the short bowel syndrome.

questions.note:
Short bowel syndrome. Removing a large part of the small intestine leaves too little absorptive surface, so the patient becomes malabsorptive and often needs nutritional support. Common causes are Crohn disease, bowel injury and cancer in adults, and necrotizing enterocolitis or atresia in infants.
Cystic fibrosis is a CFTR mutation causing pancreatic insufficiency, not a surgical loss of bowel.
Whipple disease is an infection with Tropheryma whipplei.
SIBO is bacterial overgrowth from stasis or dysmotility. Resection can set it up, but it is not the name for the malabsorption that resection causes.
Celiac disease is gluten-triggered villous atrophy with the bowel still in place.

questions.stem: From the lecture's matching exercise: which condition is characterized by foamy macrophage formation, obstruction of the lymphatic system and decreased chylomicron uptake?

evidence.quote: If somebody has this whipper disease, there is a macrophage, foamy macrophages are formed. And this entire system, now, lymphatic system gets obstructed, and that will lead to decreased absorption of chylomicron and mild digestion of fat.

questions.note:
Whipple disease. Tropheryma whipplei infiltrates the small bowel and draws in foamy macrophages (strongly PAS-positive), which block the lymphatics so chylomicrons can't be taken up and fat is malabsorbed. It is most common in middle-aged men and is treated with antibiotics.
Cystic fibrosis blocks the pancreatic ducts with thick secretions, not the intestinal lymphatics.
SIBO causes fat maldigestion because bacteria deconjugate bile acids, not through macrophages.
Celiac disease shows intraepithelial lymphocytes and flat villi, not foamy macrophages.
Short bowel syndrome is loss of absorptive length after resection.

questions.stem: From the lecture's matching exercise: which condition is linked to intestinal dysmotility?

evidence.quote: And so there are a number of diverse conditions that can lead to cybo, and majority of these are caused by intestinal dysmotility.
A number of seemingly diverse conditions lead to SIBO. The majority are caused by intestinal dysmotility.

questions.note:
SIBO. Normal motility sweeps bacteria out of the small bowel, so when motility slows (for example, autonomic neuropathy in type 1 diabetes) contents stagnate and bacteria overgrow. The result is fat maldigestion, B12 deficiency and carbohydrate malabsorption.
Cystic fibrosis is defined by CFTR dysfunction and pancreatic insufficiency, not dysmotility.
Whipple disease is an infection marked by foamy macrophages in the mucosa.
Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that flattens the villi.
Short bowel syndrome is defined by surgical loss of bowel length.

questions.stem: From the lecture's matching exercise: which condition presents with cough, diarrhea, recurrent respiratory tract infections and bulky, foul-smelling stools?

evidence.quote: Cybo, and cough, diarrhea, recurrent respiratory tract infections, bulk bulky, foul smelling stools, that is cystic fibrosis.

questions.note:
Cystic fibrosis. A CFTR mutation makes thick secretions in both the airways and the pancreas, so the patient has recurrent lung infections plus pancreatic insufficiency with bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools. The lung involvement is what sets it apart from the others.
Whipple disease causes malabsorption, fever and joint pain, but not recurrent respiratory infections from childhood.
SIBO causes malabsorption but no lung disease.
Celiac disease causes steatorrhea and diarrhea, but not cough and repeated chest infections.
Short bowel syndrome follows bowel resection and has no respiratory component.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy comes to your office with a 3-month history of chronic diarrhea. His parents tried a milk-free diet without benefit. He seems increasingly clingy and cranky with his mother. His stools are light in color, bulky and foul smelling, and occur 3 times daily. Family history is negative for GI disease. Both parents are of short stature, his mother has hypothyroidism, and his older sister has type 1 diabetes mellitus. On exam, his height is at the 25th percentile and his weight is below the 3rd percentile for age, and he is very irritable. Mild anemia is seen, with iron and folate deficiency and a low vitamin E level. IgA tissue transglutaminase is >100, antiendomysial antibody is positive, and stool studies are positive for fecal fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?

evidence.quote: Vitamin E level is decreased, and most importantly, transglutaminase they had given you. So, and again, they also showed you that stool studies, they have fecal fat. So what is the most likely diagnosis? Celiac, right?

questions.note:
Celiac disease. The positive IgA anti-tTG (>100) and antiendomysial antibody clinch it, and everything else fits. He has steatorrhea, failure to thrive, iron and folate deficiency from proximal small-bowel damage, and a low fat-soluble vitamin. The family history of autoimmune disease (hypothyroidism, type 1 diabetes) matters because these conditions share HLA-DQ2/DQ8. A failed milk-free diet rules out simple lactose intolerance.
Dumping syndrome happens after gastric surgery, which this toddler has not had.
SIBO causes steatorrhea, but folate tends to be high, not low, and it doesn't make celiac antibodies.
Whipple disease is an infection mostly of middle-aged men and would not give positive tTG or endomysial antibodies.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl dies of a respiratory infection with respiratory failure. She had had recurrent pulmonary infections since the age of 1 year. Her history showed steatorrhea, and she was taking nutritional supplements. Which of the following is most likely to be observed in the pancreas at autopsy?
choices: Significant enlargement of the pancreatic acini
Fibrosis of the islets of Langerhans
Mucous plugging of the pancreatic ducts

evidence.quote: What do you think? Mucous plugging, right? That was our buzzword.
In addition, reduced water content of secretions, precipitation of proteins, and plugging of ductules and acini, prevent the pancreatic enzymes from reaching the gut.

questions.note:
Mucous plugging of the pancreatic ducts. This is cystic fibrosis: defective CFTR lowers the water and bicarbonate in pancreatic secretions, so proteins precipitate and plug the ductules and acini, and enzymes can't reach the gut, which causes the steatorrhea. The professor called mucous plugging the buzzword.
The acini are not enlarged. Blocked ducts make the exocrine pancreas atrophy and scar.
Fibrosis in CF hits the exocrine pancreas first. The islets are spared until late, and that is not the classic finding.
Macrophage infiltration of the islets is not a feature of CF.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of this rash, which is also located on her buttocks. She admits to occasional crampy abdominal pain and bloating. What is the most likely diagnosis?

evidence.quote: What is the most likely diagnosis? What does she have? Celiac? And what is this rash called? Hepatitis der dermatitis herpetiformis, so that's how it looks like.

questions.note:
Celiac disease. The itchy papulovesicular rash on the extensor elbows and buttocks is dermatitis herpetiformis, which is 100% associated with celiac disease. The crampy pain and bloating are its GI side.
Crohn disease has skin lesions too, but they are erythema nodosum (tender red nodules on the shins) and pyoderma gangrenosum, not grouped vesicles on the elbows.
Whipple disease causes malabsorption, fever and arthralgia, not dermatitis herpetiformis.
Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhea after dairy but has no skin findings.
